content: Dental erosion refers to the loss of tooth structure caused by chemical dissolution due to acids that are not of bacterial origin. This process typically begins in the enamel, the outermost layer of the tooth, and, if left untreated, can progress to the underlying dentin. The most common cause of dental erosion is the consumption of acidic foods and beverages. Numerous clinical and laboratory studies have established a strong link between dental erosion and the excessive intake of soft drinks, including fruit juices, fruit drinks, and carbonated beverages like colas. Dental erosion is a notable feature in individuals with bulimia, as repeated vomiting exposes the oral cavity to gastric acids. The characteristic appearance of erosion often includes broad, rounded concavities on the tooth surfaces. Additionally, there may be signs of wear on areas of the teeth that are not typically in contact with one another. In children, dental erosion can result in the loss of the normal surface characteristics of enamel. In cases of dental erosion, amalgam restorations in the mouth may appear clean and untarnished, which can be a diagnostic clue. Perimolysis is commonly observed in individuals who vomit frequently or experience gastroesophageal reflux, such as patients with anorexia nervosa, bulimia, or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
